native_result.query: How does the median wealth of white individuals compare to that of black and Hispanic individuals from 1985 onwards?
native_result.HypoA: 1985 onwards, white individuals have a significantly higher median wealth compared to black and Hispanic individuals.
native_result.HypoB: Hypothesis: From 1985 onward, the median family net wealth of non-Black, non-Hispanic respondents — the only available proxy for 'white' individuals in this dataset (1979 racial/ethnic cohort code 3) — is consistently and substantially higher than that of Black and Hispanic respondents, and the gap widens over time. In 1985, median family net wealth was $3,500 for non-Black non-Hispanic respondents (n=5,774), versus $1,600 for Black respondents (n=1,699) and $500 for Hispanic respondents (n=2,631) — about 2.2 times the Black median and 7 times the Hispanic median. By 1990 the gap had widened to $12,972 (n=5,336) versus $4,800 (n=1,528) and $1,600 (n=2,431) — about 2.7× and 8.1×. By 1996 it reached $42,600 (n=3,557), roughly 4.4× the Black median of $9,800 (n=1,368) and about 16.6× the Hispanic median of $2,563 (n=2,114). Caveats: (a) 'white' is operationalized as the 1979 non-Black non-Hispanic cohort, which also includes other non-Hispanic, non-Black groups, and race is recorded only once, in 1979; (b) wealth is family/household net wealth, not individual wealth; (c) figures are nominal dollars with no deflator available in the file, so part of the widening gap reflects inflation; (d) medians are unweighted and computed on shrinking, differentially attrited samples — retention of the 1979 cohort with observed wealth was 76.9%→71.1%→47.4% (non-Black non-Hispanic), 84.9%→76.3%→68.3% (Black), and 82.9%→76.6%→66.6% (Hispanic) across 1985→1990→1996 — so later-wave gaps may be biased in either direction and cannot be corrected without weights.
